definitions.text: A Jew. [Slang or Colloq.] "Almost any young Yid who goes out from among her people." John Corbin.
A language used by German and other Jews, being a Middle German dialect developed under Hebrew and Slavic influence. It is written in Hebrew characters.
A Yid. [Slang]

To give in return for labor expended; to produce, as payment or interest on what is expended or invested; to pay; as, money at interest yields six or seven per cent. To yelde Jesu Christ his proper rent. Chaucer. When thou tillest the ground, it shall not henceforth yield unto thee her strength. Gen. iv. 12.
To furnish; to afford; to render; to give forth. "Vines yield nectar." Milton. [He] makes milch kine yield blood. Shak. The wilderness yieldeth food for them and for their children. Job xxiv. 5.

To give up, as something that is claimed or demanded; to make over to one who has a claim or right; to resign; to surrender; to relinquish; as a city, an opinion, etc. And, force perforce, I'll make him yield the crown. Shak. Shall yield up all their virtue, all their fame. Milton.
To admit to be true; to concede; to allow. I yield it just, said Adam, and submit. Milton.
To permit; to grant; as, to yield passage.

To give a reward to; to bless. [Obs.] Chaucer. Tend me to-night two hours, I ask no more, And the gods yield you for 't. Shak. God yield thee, and God thank ye. Beau. & Fl. To yield the breath, the ghost, or the life, to die; to expire; -- often followed by up. One calmly yields his willing breath. Keble.
To give up the contest; to submit; to surrender; to succumb. He saw the fainting Grecians yield. Dryden.
To comply with; to assent; as, I yielded to his request.

To give way; to cease opposition; to be no longer a hindrance or an obstacle; as, men readily yield to the current of opinion, or to customs; the door yielded. Will ye relent, And yield to mercy while 't is offered you Shak.
To give place, as inferior in rank or excellence; as, they will yield to us in nothing. Nay tell me first, in what more happy fields The thistle springs, to which the lily yields Pope.
Amount yielded; product; -- applied especially to products resulting from growth or cultivation. "A goodly yield of fruit doth bring." Bacon.
Disposed to yield or comply. [R.] -- Yield"a*ble*ness, n. [R.] Bp. Hall.
The act of producing; yield; as, the yieldance of the earth. [R.] Bp. Hall.
The act of yielding; concession. [R.] South.
One who yields. Shak.

Inclined to give way, or comply; flexible; compliant; accommodating; as, a yielding temper. Yielding and paying (Law), the initial words of that clause in leases in which the rent to be paid by the lessee is mentioned and reserved. Burrill. attentive or yielding in a high degree without any sacrifice of his dignity; but he who is obsequious seeks to gain favor by excessive and mean compliances for some selfish end.
Without yielding; unyielding. [Obs.]
Gift. [Obs.] "Great yiftes." Chaucer.
A Chinese weight of 2
Yes. [Obs.] "Yis, sir," quod he, "yis, host." Chaucer.
Yet. [Obs.] Chaucer.
The European yellow-hammer.
To give. [Obs.] Chaucer. -YL -yl. Etym: [Gr. (Chem.)

A suffix used as a characteristic termination of chemical radicals; as in ethyl, carbonyl, hydroxyl, etc. benzoyl, in the sense of stuff, or fundamental material, then in 1834 by Dumas and Peligot in naming methyl, in the sense of wood. After this -yl was generally used as in benzoyl, in the sense of stuff, characteristic ground, fundamental material.
